Group action (G×X⟶X)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra Group theory
OurBigBook.com Words: 11k Articles: 110
A left group action of a group G on a set X is a function (g,x)↦g⋅x satisfying
e⋅x=x,(gh)⋅x=g⋅(h⋅x)(g,h∈G, x∈X),
(1)
where e is the identity element of G. The second rule means that h moves the point first and g moves it next. These rules let group multiplication describe consistent rearrangements of a set; see Ackerman's algebra notes, definition 0.4.1.1.
For each g, the function x↦g⋅x is a bijection: its inverse is x↦g−1⋅x, using the inverse element of g. Equivalently, a group action is a group homomorphism ρ:G→Sym(X) into the symmetric group of all permutations of X, with ρ(g)(x)=g⋅x and ρ(gh)=ρ(g)∘ρ(h). See MIT's group-action notes, definition 23.1.
For a concrete group action, put the vertices of a polygon of a square at A=(1,1), B=(−1,1), C=(−1,−1) and D=(1,−1). Let r(x,y)=(−y,x) be a counterclockwise quarter-turn rotation and let s(x,y)=(y,x) be a reflection. Their eight permutations of the vertices of a polygon form the dihedral group
D4​={e,r,r2,r3,s,rs,r2s,r3s},r4=s2=e,srs=r−1.
(2)
Here D4​ means the symmetry group of a four-sided polygon, with group order eight; the alternative convention calls this same group D8​. Products apply the rightmost operation first. For example, s⋅B=D and (rs)⋅B=r⋅D=A. The same group also has separate group actions on the sides of a polygon, the diagonals of a polygon, and the singleton set containing the centroid of the square. Specifying X matters: changing what is moved changes the orbits of a group action and the stabilizer subgroups.
A group action need not be a faithful group action. For example, the cyclic group C4​=Z/4Z acts on X={0,1} by k⋅x=x+k(mod2), using modular arithmetic. Only the parity of k matters: 0,2 fix both points and 1,3 exchange them. The associated group homomorphism C4​→Sym(X) has group kernel {0,2}, of group order two. Either point has a group orbit of size two and a stabilizer subgroup of group order two, so the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives 4=2⋅2.
The useful questions are which positions can be exchanged, and which transformations survive after imposing a constraint such as keeping one marked point fixed. An orbit of a group action answers the first question; a stabilizer subgroup answers the second. This turns a list of transformations into a count of distinct configurations, and explains why several transformations can produce the same configuration.

n-transitive group action (n-transitive)

Words: 42
Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action on a set is n-transitive when it can send any ordered tuple of n distinct points to any other such tuple. Here ordered means a sequence of entries, not increasing in a total order. For order-preserving actions the corresponding notion is order n-transitivity.

Symmetry enlargement under group translates (S=⋃g∈G​g(T))

Words: 67
Group action OurBigBook.com
For a group of Euclidean isometries, every element preserves the displayed union of images of a set, because left multiplication permutes its group indices. Its full setwise isometry group can be larger even when T itself has no nonidentity symmetry. Take G to be the integer translations of the plane and T={(0,0),(1,0),(0,2)}. By rigidity of a scalene triangle, T has trivial stabilizer subgroup. Yet S=Z2, whose quarter-turn about the origin is a symmetry outside the translation group.

Subgroup factorization from coset transitivity (G=HK⟺K is transitive on H\G)

Words: 48
Group action OurBigBook.com
In the right multiplication action, the orbit of the coset H under K is {Hk:k∈K}. It is the whole right coset space exactly when every g has form hk, proving the displayed criterion. The factorization need not be unique; for finite groups ∣HK∣=∣H∣∣K∣/∣H∩K∣.

Symmetry group (Aut(X))

Words: 806 Articles: 3
Group action OurBigBook.com
A symmetry group collects bijections of an object to itself that preserve a specified structure in both directions, with function composition as the operation. For a geometric object one may require Euclidean distances to be preserved, giving an isometry group; for a graph, one preserves adjacency, giving a graph automorphism group. For an unstructured finite set, every permutation is allowed. The structure to be preserved is part of the definition.
For a square with its usual geometric structure, the symmetry group consists of four rotations and four reflections. These form the dihedral group of group order eight. The existing group action example shows how its eight elements move the vertices of a polygon; changing the object to its edges or a marked configuration changes the group action being studied.[ref]
Specifying the preserved data makes it possible to test a proposed symmetry exactly. After the preserved data are declared, function composition, the identity map, and inverse maps automatically preserve them too. Symmetry transformations therefore form a group, and questions about equivalent configurations become questions about group orbits, stabilizer subgroups, and group homomorphisms. This supplies reusable mathematics for comparing many different kinds of objects.

Symmetry transformation

Words: 22
Symmetry group OurBigBook.com
A symmetry transformation is a bijection preserving the data that define the object's symmetry group. Its individual group elements are symmetry transformations; the group operation combines them by function composition.

Symmetry depends on preserved structure (∣Gset​∣=24,∣Gaffine​∣=8,∣Gmetric​∣=4)

Words: 350
Symmetry group OurBigBook.com
Take the four-point set
R={(2,1),(−2,1),(−2,−1),(2,−1)},
(3)
the vertices of a polygon of a rectangle whose side lengths are four and two. Three choices of structure give three different symmetry groups on these same points.
As an unstructured set, R has all 4!=24 permutations as symmetries, forming the symmetric group S4​. If Euclidean distance is part of the data, the allowed maps are only the identity, a half-turn rotation, and the reflections across the two coordinate axes. They form a Klein four-group of group order four. To see that nothing is missing, fix the image of one vertex of a polygon: its three other distances, 2, 4, and 20​, are distinct, so they uniquely determine the images of the remaining vertices.
Preserving affine structure permits more. The affine map
T(x,y)=(−2y,x/2),T=(01/2​−20​)
(4)
cycles all four points of R. It sends a horizontal side of length four to a vertical side of length two, so it is not an isometry. Yet it preserves the rectangle's vertex set and all affine combinations among those points.
Let A=diag(2,1) and let r(x,y)=(−y,x) be the square's quarter-turn rotation. Then
T=ArA−1.
(5)
Conjugating every square symmetry by A gives eight affine maps preserving R. This group isomorphism makes the affine symmetry group a dihedral group, although some of its maps do not preserve the original Euclidean distances. There are no further affine symmetries: an affine map preserves the common midpoint of the diagonals, so it must preserve opposite pairs. The image of one vertex has four choices and the image of an adjacent vertex has two; those choices determine the map through three noncollinear points.
Thus
Gmetric​⊊Gaffine​⊊Gset​,4<8<24.​
(6)
An arbitrary permutation need not be an affine map. For example, exchanging the two top vertices while fixing the two bottom vertices sends the common diagonal midpoint to two different points, which no single affine map can do. The phrase "the symmetry of these points" becomes unambiguous only after stating which structure matters.

Colour-preserving symmetry group (Gc​={g∈G:c(gx)=c(x) for all x∈X})

Words: 262
Symmetry group OurBigBook.com
Let a group action of G on a set X be given, and let a function c:X→C attach a colour label to each point. The colour-preserving subgroup of G is
Gc​={g∈G:c(gx)=c(x) for every x∈X}.
(7)
It is a subgroup: the identity map preserves all labels, compositions of two preserving maps preserve them, and replacing x by g−1x shows that inverse maps preserve them too. Extra object data restrict the allowable transformations; the labels are now part of the object rather than bookkeeping for a drawing.
For a geometric square, take G=D4​, of group order eight. If all four vertices have the same colour, all eight maps remain. If two adjacent vertices are red and the others blue, only the identity and one reflection remain. Putting the two red vertices opposite one another instead leaves four maps: the identity, a half-turn rotation, and the two diagonal reflections. Giving all four vertices distinct colours leaves only the identity.
The count alone does not specify the pattern. Both two-red examples have the same number of red and blue vertices, but their stabilizer subgroups differ. For a single red vertex, the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives a group orbit of size four and a stabilizer subgroup of group order two, agreeing with the existing group action illustration. Such counts identify equivalent placements without treating each placement as a new geometric case.

Finite support in a permutation action (G(S)​⊆Stab(x),∣S∣<∞)

Words: 89
Group action OurBigBook.com
Suppose a permutation group G acts on an underlying atom set A and on a collection of objects built over it. A finite subset S⊆A supports an object x when every permutation fixing all members of S fixes x. Pairing supported objects uses the union of their supports. A definable subset or functional image inherits a support from its domain and parameters. In a hereditarily finite-supported Quine-atom model, every member is recursively required to have such a support; symmetry then rules out a choice function on the pairs of atoms.

Free action of a group (gx=x⟹g=1)

Words: 56
Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action is free when only the identity fixes any given point, or equivalently every stabilizer subgroup is trivial. The trivial group acts freely on every space. A nontrivial group acting freely must act by a fixed-point-free map for each nonidentity element; the fixed-point property of even-dimensional complex projective space obstructs such actions. For a finite group acting freely on a Hausdorff manifold, the quotient map is a covering map.

Free group action (gx=x⟹g=1)

Words: 610 Articles: 3
Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action is free if the only element of the group fixing any point is the identity element. Thus every stabilizer subgroup is trivial. This is a property of an action of any group, not an assertion that the acting group is a free group.
Explicitly, for a left group action of a group G on a set X with identity element e, freeness means
g⋅x=x⟹g=e(g∈G, x∈X),Gx​={e}(x∈X).
(8)
Equivalently, for any x,y∈X there is at most one g∈G with g⋅x=y. Indeed, if g⋅x=h⋅x, the group action rules give (h−1g)⋅x=x, so freeness forces g=h; conversely, take y=x, since the identity element already sends x to itself. Thus every orbit map g↦g⋅x is injective, even when its image of a function is only part of X.
For a permutation example, let the cyclic group C2​={e,a} act on the set X={1,2,3,4} by a=(12)(34). The nonidentity element exchanges both pairs and fixes no point, so every stabilizer subgroup is {e}. Its two group orbits are {1,2} and {3,4}. This is a free group action but not a transitive group action: there is no group element sending 1 to 3. Each restriction to one group orbit is a simply transitive group action.
The identity element fixes every point in every group action; freeness excludes fixed points only for nonidentity elements. This also differs from a fixed point of a group action, which must be fixed by every group element. In the left diagram there are no such fixed points of a group action. In the right diagram, the same abstract cyclic group C2​ acts by e⋅x=a⋅x=x: all four points are fixed points of a group action, every stabilizer subgroup is C2​, and each group orbit is a singleton set. Consequently this second group action is neither free nor transitive. A group action with no fixed points of a group action can still fail freeness: the natural group action of the symmetric group S3​ has no point fixed by all of S3​, but (23) fixes 1.
For a finite group, the orbit-stabilizer theorem makes each group orbit of a free group action have cardinality ∣G∣. If X is also finite, ∣X∣ is therefore a multiple of the group order, with one copy of ∣G∣ for each group orbit. The trivial group acts freely on every set, and acts transitively exactly on a singleton set. On the empty set freeness is vacuous; our convention under transitive group action requires a nonempty set for transitivity.

Finite groups cannot act freely on Euclidean space

Words: 70
Free group action OurBigBook.com
If a nontrivial finite group acted freely on Rn, a prime-order cyclic subgroup Cp​ would too. The quotient is an n-manifold with contractible universal cover. The singular version of cellular free resolution from a contractible universal cover identifies its cohomology with group cohomology of Cp​. The periodic resolution of a finite cyclic group gives H2j(Cp​;Z)=Z/p for every j≥1. But Poincaré duality for noncompact manifolds makes the quotient cohomology zero above dimension n. This contradiction excludes the action, for arbitrary homeomorphisms, not only Euclidean isometries.

Free actions on even-dimensional spheres have order at most two

Words: 67
Free group action OurBigBook.com
For every nonidentity element of a free group action on S2r, its action map has no fixed point and hence degree minus one by fixed-point-free sphere maps are homotopic to the antipodal map. Degree of homeomorphisms defines a homomorphism into {1,−1}, whose kernel is trivial, since no nonidentity action map can have degree one. Thus the acting group has order at most two. For S0, freeness on its two points gives the same conclusion directly.

Free sphere actions exclude elementary abelian subgroups of rank two (Cp​×Cp​↷free​Sn(n>1))

Words: 94
Free group action OurBigBook.com
Suppose a finite group G acts freely on Sn, n>1. The quotient has fundamental group G and higher homotopy groups equal to those of Sn. Attach one (n+1)-cell killing a generator of πn​≅Z, then attach higher cells successively to kill all remaining higher homotopy. This constructs a Eilenberg–MacLane space K(G,1) with only one (n+1)-cell. The one-cell bound on next-degree cohomology gives dimension at most one in degree n+1. But if G=Cp​×Cp​, the mod-p cohomology ring of a cyclic group and Künneth theorem give dimension n+2 there. This contradiction excludes that group, and also excludes such a subgroup of any group acting freely on a sphere.

Fundamental domain (F)

Words: 62
Group action OurBigBook.com
For a group action, a fundamental domain selects one representative from each orbit. Geometric fundamental domains are often taken with their boundary included, allowing boundary overlaps while their interiors remain disjoint under the action. For translations of the real line by the integers, [0,1) is an exact representative set and [0,1] is its closed geometric version. A lattice similarly gives a half-open fundamental parallelepiped.

Multiply transitive group action (t-transitive)

Words: 68 Articles: 1
Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action is t-transitive if it acts transitively on ordered t-tuples of distinct points. In degree n≥t this implies n(n−1)⋯(n−t+1)∣∣G∣. It is sharply t-transitive when each such ordered tuple has trivial stabilizer subgroup.

Three-transitive group action

Words: 34
Multiply transitive group action OurBigBook.com
Transitivity on ordered triples of distinct points. It implies a two-transitive group action, but is stronger: in projective dimension at least two, collinear and noncollinear triples distinguish two orbits, even though the projective action is two-transitive.

Diagonal action on a centerless group ((a,b):t↦a−1tb)

Words: 57
Group action OurBigBook.com
For nontrivial centerless T, this action of T×T is faithful and transitive. Its identity stabilizer is the diagonal subgroup. Subgroups above that diagonal are {(a,b):a−1b∈N} with N⊴T: multiply by a diagonal element to isolate the second coordinate, then use diagonal conjugation. Thus the action is primitive exactly when T is nonabelian simple.

Ring of invariants (RG={r:g(r)=r for every g∈G})

Words: 133 Articles: 1
Group action OurBigBook.com
For a group acting on a ring by ring automorphisms, the elements fixed by every group element form a subring containing 1. For finite G acting on a commutative ring, each r satisfies the monic orbit equation ∏g∈G​(T−g(r)), whose coefficients are fixed. Thus R is integral over its invariant subring. This uses an orbit product, not division by the group order.

Normality of a ring of invariants (R normal domain⟹RG normal domain)

Words: 73
Ring of invariants OurBigBook.com
A fraction of invariant elements is fixed by every automorphism. If that fraction is integral over RG, its monic equation also makes it integral over R. A normal domain therefore places it in R, and fixedness places it in RG. This proves integral closedness of the invariant subring in its own fraction field. The proof works for any group and in every characteristic; no averaging or finiteness of the group is needed for normality.

Primitive group action

Words: 510 Articles: 7
Group action OurBigBook.com
A transitive group action is primitive if the only blocks are singletons and the whole set; a block has every translate either equal to it or disjoint from it. Orbits of a normal subgroup form blocks. Hence a nontrivial normal subgroup in a faithful primitive action is transitive. Two-transitivity implies primitivity. This normal-subgroup observation is a hypothesis engine for Iwasawa's simplicity lemma.

Primitive group with a transposition

Words: 54
Primitive group action OurBigBook.com
If a primitive subgroup of Sn​ contains a transposition, make a graph whose edges are the supports of its conjugate transpositions. Connected components form blocks for the group. An edge exists, so primitivity forces the graph to be connected. Its edge transpositions generate all of Sn​, proving that the original group is Sn​.

Even primitive groups of safe-prime degree (p=2q+1, q prime: G≤Ap​⟹G simple or ∣G∣=pq)

Words: 93
Primitive group action OurBigBook.com
Every nontrivial normal subgroup of a faithful primitive group of prime degree is transitive and contains a Sylow p-subgroup P. Its normalizer in Ap​ has order pq. For a proper normal subgroup N, the Frattini argument gives G=NNG​(P); unless G=Cp​, its P-normalizer is the full order-pq normalizer, while NN​(P)=P. The Burnside transfer theorem gives a characteristic normal p-complement in N. This complement is normal in G and cannot be transitive because its order is prime to p, so it is trivial. Thus N=P and ∣G∣=pq.

O'Nan–Scott theorem

Words: 279 Articles: 3
Primitive group action OurBigBook.com
The theorem classifies finite primitive permutation groups by their minimal normal subgroups and the action of their socle. The modern types are affine (HA), almost simple (AS), simple diagonal (SD), compound diagonal (CD), product action (PA), holomorph simple (HS), holomorph compound (HC), and twisted wreath (TW). A coarser version describes primitive maximal subgroups of symmetric groups by affine, almost-simple, diagonal and full product-action overgroups. Intransitive and imprimitive maxima are respectively unequal-part subset stabilizers and block-system stabilizers. Primitivity alone is not maximality in the symmetric group; parity can put an otherwise natural candidate entirely inside the alternating group.

Diagonal primitive permutation group (n=∣T∣r−1,Tr∩Gα​=diag(T))

Words: 89
O'Nan–Scott theorem OurBigBook.com
For a nonabelian simple group T, act on cosets of its full diagonal in Tr. A suitable factor-permuting extension is primitive and has point stabilizer intersecting the socle in the diagonal. The full normalizer has order ∣T∣r∣Out(T)∣r!. For T=A5​,r=2, it acts on the sixty elements of A5​ by left/right multiplication, automorphisms and inversion, and has order 14400. Odd conjugation in S5​ induces an odd permutation of these sixty points, while inversion is even; the full group is a primitive maximal subgroup of S60​.

Affine primitive permutation group (G=Fpd​⋊H,H≤GLd​(p) irreducible)

Words: 93 Articles: 1
O'Nan–Scott theorem OurBigBook.com
An elementary abelian regular minimal normal subgroup acts as translations of a vector space. Its point stabilizer acts faithfully and irreducibly on that space; invariant subspaces would be blocks. The full affine normalizer is AGLd​(p). In degree sixteen it lies inside A16​: nonzero translations swap eight pairs, and elementary linear transvections swap four pairs. Thus it is not a maximal subgroup of S16​.
General affine group (AGLd​(p)=Fpd​⋊GLd​(p))
Words: 27
Affine primitive permutation group OurBigBook.com
The group of maps x↦Ax+b of a finite-dimensional vector space, with A invertible. Identifying the underlying points with a regular elementary abelian group identifies its normalizer in the symmetric group with this semidirect product.

Words: 24
Primitive group action OurBigBook.com
Conjugate the three-cycle throughout the group. Connected components of the support hypergraph form an invariant block system. Primitivity makes it connected, and connected triple supports generate an alternating group gives the conclusion.

Variable-permutation action on polynomials ((σ⋅f)(x)=f(xσ(1)​,…,xσ(n)​))

Words: 43
Group action OurBigBook.com
The symmetric group acts on multivariate polynomials by replacing each variable xi​ by xσ(i)​. With (στ)(i)=σ(τ(i)), substitution gives σ⋅(τ⋅f)=(στ)⋅f. Thus it is a left group action. A polynomial encoding a combinatorial partition has a group orbit encoding all relabelings and a stabiliser subgroup encoding its label symmetries.

Fixed point of a group action (AG)

Words: 38
Group action OurBigBook.com
A fixed point of a group action is an element fixed by every group element. The set AG={a:g⋅a=a for all g∈G} is the categorical limit of the action viewed as a functor from the one-object category associated with G to the Category of sets.

Left regular action (g⋅h=gh)

Words: 37
Group action OurBigBook.com
The left regular action of a group on its own underlying set is left multiplication. It is faithful, because an element fixing the identity is itself the identity. For a finite group it gives the permutation representation used in Cayley theorem.

Block system

Words: 162 Articles: 1
Group action OurBigBook.com
A block system for a group action is a partition of the acted-on set such that every group element permutes its parts. For a transitive action, a nontrivial block system has more than one part and more than one element per part. The full symmetric group preserves no such partition: a transposition exchanging one point in each of two parts breaks it.

Uniform subdegrees force an imprimitive action to be Frobenius

Words: 106
Block system OurBigBook.com
For a transitive finite permutation group, suppose each point stabilizer has orbits of a common size r on the other points. If a nontrivial block system exists, all two-point stabilizers are trivial. Indeed for block size b, r∣n−1 gives gcd(r,b)=1. An orbit of a block not containing α has size at most br and divisible by br, so its b point-orbits are disjoint. A stabilizer of α and a point of that block fixes the whole block. Interchanging the two points also fixes the block of α. Equal two-point-stabilizer orders then show that each two-point stabilizer fixes every point, and faithfulness makes it trivial.

Transitive group action

Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action on a nonempty set X is transitive when every two points lie in the same orbit of a group action, equivalently when for all x,y∈X there is a group element g with g⋅x=y. There is exactly one group orbit: every position is reachable from every other. Requiring X=∅ avoids calling the group action on the empty set transitive merely because the quantified statement has no points to test.[ref]
Here a left group action of a group G means a function G×X→X, written (g,x)↦g⋅x, satisfying
e⋅x=x,(gh)⋅x=g⋅(h⋅x),
(9)
where e is the identity element. Products move the point by h first, then by g. Transitivity says that an orbit map G→X, g↦g⋅x, is surjective for every x∈X; it suffices to check one chosen point.[ref][ref]
For example, the symmetric group S3​ acts on X={1,2,3} by σ⋅i=σ(i). This is a transitive group action, but it is not a free group action: the stabilizer subgroup of 1 is {e,(23)}. Both the transposition (12) and the cyclic permutation (123) send 1 to 2. In contrast, the cyclic group C3​=Z/3Z acts on itself by k⋅x=k+x(mod3), using modular arithmetic. The group element sending x to y is uniquely k=y−x(mod3). These two group actions reach the same number of points, but only the second has unique transport between them.
The stabilizer subgroup Gx​={h∈G:h⋅x=x} measures the ambiguity of transport. If g0​⋅x=y, then
{g∈G:g⋅x=y}=g0​Gx​,Gy​=g0​Gx​g0−1​.
(10)
The first set is a left coset, and the second identity says that stabilizer subgroups in one group orbit are conjugate subgroups. Briefly, g⋅x=g0​⋅x exactly when g0−1​g∈Gx​. Thus, for a finite group in a transitive group action, the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives ∣G∣=∣X∣∣Gx​∣, and there are exactly ∣Gx​∣ transports for each pair of points. The example counts are 6=3⋅2 for S3​ and 3=3⋅1 for C3​. This separates the number of reachable positions from the number of ways to reach each one.[ref]

Simply transitive group action (∀x,y ∃!g: gx=y)

Words: 296
Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A group action on a nonempty set X is simply transitive when exactly one group element sends any chosen point to any other:
∀x,y∈X∃!g∈G:g⋅x=y.
(11)
Equivalently it is both a transitive group action and a free group action; this is also a regular group action. Transitivity supplies a transport, and freeness makes it unique. Conversely, putting y=x in the uniqueness condition shows that every stabilizer subgroup is {e}, since the identity element already fixes x. In a transitive group action, checking that just one stabilizer subgroup is trivial suffices: all the others are conjugate subgroups.
The cyclic group C3​ in the diagram under transitive group action is simply transitive. More generally, the left regular action of any group G on itself is simply transitive: the equation gx=y has the unique solution g=yx−1, using the inverse element of x. This shows why the property is useful: every position has a unique label relative to a chosen starting position.
Choose a point x0​∈X. Its orbit map
ϕx0​​:G⟶X,g⟼g⋅x0​
(12)
is a bijection and an equivariant map from the left regular action: ϕx0​​(hg)=h⋅ϕx0​​(g). This identifies X with a copy of G, but X does not come with a preferred identity element. If x1​=a⋅x0​, then ϕx1​​(g)=ϕx0​​(ga): changing the chosen point composes this identification with right multiplication by a. An old label g therefore becomes the new label ga−1, which also specifies the side of multiplication for a noncommutative group.
The transport from x to y remains independent of the chosen point. Writing x=b⋅x0​ and y=c⋅x0​, it is cb−1. With x1​=a⋅x0​, the new labels are ba−1 and ca−1, and
(ca−1)(ba−1)−1=cb−1.
(13)
For a finite group, simple transitivity implies ∣X∣=∣G∣. Conversely, a transitive group action with ∣X∣=∣G∣<∞ is simply transitive by the orbit-stabilizer theorem. Equality of cardinalities alone is insufficient without transitivity: the cyclic group C2​ can fix both points of a two-point set, giving two group orbits and two possible self-transports at each point.

Regular group action (Gω​=1)

Words: 63
Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A transitive group action is regular if every point stabilizer is trivial. Equivalently each ordered pair of points is connected by exactly one group element. Identifying one point with the identity identifies the action with left multiplication on the group. A regular normal subgroup inside a larger primitive group can supply translations or nonabelian left multiplication; the whole primitive group usually has a nontrivial stabilizer acting by automorphisms of this regular subgroup.

Derangement in a transitive group action (Fix(g)=∅)

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A derangement is an element fixing none of the points of a group action. Every finite transitive action on at least two points has a derangement. Count pairs (g,x) with gx=x: transitivity gives ∑g​∣Fix(g)∣=∑x​∣Gx​∣=∣G∣. If every element fixed a point, the identity's extra fixed points would make this sum strictly larger than ∣G∣. This is the Burnside lemma counting argument specialized to existence of a derangement.

Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A regular permutation subgroup acts transitively with trivial point stabilizers. Each ordered pair of points is related by exactly one subgroup element. A finite regular subgroup on n points has order n. Normality and characteristicity are additional properties; they do not follow from regularity alone.

Sharp t-transitivity (∣G∣=n(n−1)⋯(n−t+1))

Words: 217 Articles: 3
Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
An action is sharply t-transitive if each ordered t-tuple of distinct points is carried to any other by exactly one group element. For finite degree n≥t, its order is n(n−1)⋯(n−t+1) and each ordered-tuple stabilizer is trivial. Sharp one-transitivity is a regular action. Finite sharp two-transitivity gives a regular kernel of a finite sharply two-transitive group.

Sharp t-transitivity OurBigBook.com
Exactly one element sends each ordered triple of distinct points to each other such triple. On a projective line, representatives of the first two target points form a basis; scaling them so their sum represents the third point gives the unique projective transformation.

Sharp two-transitivity (∣G∣=n(n−1))

Words: 31
Sharp t-transitivity OurBigBook.com
A group action is sharply two-transitive when exactly one element sends each ordered distinct pair to each other ordered distinct pair. The affine group over a finite field provides an example: solve ax+b=u and ay+b=v uniquely, giving a=(v−u)/(y−x).

Regular kernel of a finite sharply two-transitive group

Words: 92
Sharp t-transitivity OurBigBook.com
In a finite sharply two-transitive group, the identity together with all fixed-point-free elements forms a regular normal subgroup. One proof constructs virtual characters from induced point-stabilizer characters and the augmentation character, proves their norms are one, and realizes this set as an intersection of representation kernels. Conjugation by the point stabilizer is transitive on the kernel's nonidentity elements. This forces the kernel to be elementary abelian, so it is a unique Sylow subgroup and is characteristic. Closure of the fixed-point-free set is a theorem, not something supplied merely by counting its size.

Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
Adjoin a new point ω fixed by a transitive group G. A one-point extension is a transitive group on the enlarged set whose stabilizer of ω is exactly G, acting on the remaining points in the prescribed way. Its order is (n+1)∣G∣ in the finite degree-n case. The double-coset criterion for a one-point extension gives a concrete generator test.

Prime-degree transposition criterion (G=Sp​)

Words: 85
Transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A transitive subgroup G≤Sp​ for prime p that contains a transposition is Sp​. Form a graph on the p letters with edges given by all conjugates in G of that transposition. The transitive action permutes connected components, so their common size divides p. An edge rules out size one, hence the graph is connected. Its edge transpositions generate Sp​: successive swaps along a path generate the swap of its endpoint with any chosen start. All these edge transpositions belong to G.

Two-transitive group action

Words: 301 Articles: 4
Group action OurBigBook.com
A group action on a set is two-transitive when it acts transitively on ordered pairs of distinct points. Equivalently, a point stabilizer acts transitively on the remaining points.
This is the k=2 case of a multiply transitive group action.

Elementary abelian regular kernels in doubly transitive groups

Words: 75
Two-transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A point stabilizer in a doubly transitive group acts transitively by conjugation on the nonidentity elements of a regular normal subgroup N. All those elements have the same order; Cauchy's theorem makes this a prime p and excludes other primes from ∣N∣. A finite p-group has a nontrivial characteristic center. Transitivity then forces all of N into its center, so N is elementary abelian. Choosing a vector-space basis identifies the original permutation group with a subgroup of the corresponding general affine group.

Two-transitive group action OurBigBook.com
There are (36​)/2=10 partitions of six letters into two unordered triples. A stabilizer is S3​≀S2​, also the normalizer of the Sylow subgroup generated by one 3-cycle in each triple. Relative to one partition, all other partitions have intersection pattern 1+2 up to interchange, giving one orbit of the stabilizer and hence a two-transitive action. A natural S5​ fixing one letter is transitive on these partitions, giving S6​=S5​(S3​≀S2​).

Minimal normal subgroup dichotomy for two-transitive groups

Words: 85
Two-transitive group action OurBigBook.com
A minimal normal subgroup of a finite faithful two-transitive group action is either regular elementary abelian or primitive nonabelian simple. The imprimitive case reduces to two-point stabilizers being trivial, then counting derangements gives a characteristic regular Sylow subgroup. In the primitive nonregular case, each simple direct factor is transitive. Two commuting transitive factors are regular and are mutual full centralizers. Thus at most two factors occur and ∣N∣=n2. But the common subdegree of Nα​ then divides both n and n−1, forcing Nα​=1, a contradiction. Only one factor remains.

Translations are regular on V, and the zero stabilizer is H. Two-transitivity is equivalent to H being transitive on nonzero vectors. Full affine linear groups and groups with special linear or symplectic linear parts give examples.

For a group G acting on a set X and a point x∈X, the orbit map is G→X, g↦gx. Its image is the orbit of a group action of x, and its fibres are cosets of the stabilizer subgroup of x.

Conjugation action OurBigBook.com
For a proper subgroup B of a finite group G, the number m of its conjugates is [G:NG​(B)]≤[G:B], because its normalizer contains B. All conjugates contain the identity, so their union has size at most 1+m(∣B∣−1)≤∣G∣−[G:B]+1<∣G∣. Thus some element is not conjugate to any element of B. Finiteness is essential to this cardinal counting argument.

Conjugate group elements

Conjugation OurBigBook.com
Two group elements x and y are conjugate when y=gxg−1 for some group element g, equivalently when they belong to the same conjugacy class. Conjugate elements have the same order of a group element.
Conjugate permutation

Conjugate group elements OurBigBook.com
Two permutations in the same symmetric group are conjugate if τ=πσπ−1 for some permutation π. Conjugation relabels every permutation cycle, so it preserves cycle type. Conversely, equal cycle types permit a relabelling between corresponding cycles, establishing conjugacy.

Conjugacy class (ClG​(x))

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Conjugation action OurBigBook.com
For an element x of a group G, its conjugacy class is its orbit of a group action under the conjugation action:
ClG​(x)={gxg−1:g∈G}.
(15)
Thus conjugate group elements describe the same operation after a change of labels. In a symmetric group, conjugation renames the entries of every permutation cycle:
g(a1​a2​…ak​)g−1=(g(a1​)g(a2​)…g(ak​)).
(16)
For example, with g=(123) and the transposition t=(12), this gives gtg−1=(g(1)g(2))=(23). Products use function composition of permutations, with the rightmost factor applied first. The complete six-element example is conjugacy classes of the symmetric group on three letters.
The conjugacy classes form a partition of a set of G, since conjugacy is an equivalence relation. In a symmetric group, two permutations lie in the same conjugacy class precisely when they have the same cycle type: renaming preserves the lengths of permutation cycles, and matching equal-length permutation cycles constructs a renaming in the other direction. This compresses many labelled permutations into a few structural types. See McKernan, Conjugation in Sn, lemma 6.2 and proposition 6.6.
The stabilizer subgroup of x under the conjugation action is its centralizer CG​(x). Consequently the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives
∣ClG​(x)∣=[G:CG​(x)],∣ClG​(x)∣=∣CG​(x)∣∣G∣​if G is finite.
(17)
The counting mechanism is the bijection gCG​(x)↦gxg−1 from left cosets onto the conjugacy class: two choices of g give the same result exactly when they differ on the right by an element of the centralizer. A large centralizer means many choices of labels leave the operation unchanged, hence a small conjugacy class. A conjugacy class has size one precisely when its element belongs to the center of a group. The class equation counts these orbits of a group action together.

Torsion-freeness from one nonidentity conjugacy class

Words: 77
Conjugacy class OurBigBook.com
If an infinite group has a single nonidentity conjugacy class, it is a torsion-free group. Otherwise every nonidentity element has the same finite order n. Powers show n is prime. For n≥3, choose xgx−1=g2; then xn=1 gives g=g2n, impossible by Fermat's little theorem. For n=2, the group has exponent two and is abelian, so every conjugacy class is a singleton and the hypothesis would force the group to have only two elements. Infinitude excludes this final case.

Shortest conjugacy representative

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Conjugacy class OurBigBook.com
A shortest conjugacy representative is a word having the fewest written letters among all words representing elements of a fixed conjugacy class. This minimum equals the least group word length of an element in the class; a longer spelling of that element is not itself a shortest representative. Such a word exists because lengths are nonnegative integers. It is freely and cyclically reduced: free cancellation shortens the same representative, while removing mutually inverse first and last letters shortens a conjugate. Every cyclic rotation has the same minimal length.

Shortest conjugacy representative OurBigBook.com
A nonempty shortest conjugacy representative is a cyclically reduced word. If w=svs−1 with first and last letters inverse, v is a shorter word representing a conjugate. Consequently wn has length exactly n∣w∣ as a freely reduced word, and any segment of the periodic word of length at most ∣w∣ fits in a cyclic rotation of w. This observation turns a Dehn shortening segment crossing copy boundaries into a shortening of a conjugacy representative.

For an even permutation g, its symmetric group class splits into two equal alternating group classes exactly when its symmetric-group centralizer contains no odd permutation. If an odd commuting element exists, an odd conjugator can be multiplied by it to become even; otherwise the index-two subgroup has two conjugation orbits. In cycle notation the splitting types are precisely distinct odd cycle lengths, counting fixed points as length-one cycles: rotating odd cycles is even, whereas an even cycle or the exchange of two equal odd cycles supplies an odd centralizer element.

Class equation (∣G∣=∣Z(G)∣+∑i​[G:CG​(xi​)])

Words: 261 Articles: 1
Conjugacy class OurBigBook.com
For a finite group G, choose one representative xi​ from each conjugacy class with more than one element. The class equation is
∣G∣=∣Z(G)∣+∑i​[G:CG​(xi​)]=∣Z(G)∣+∑i​∣CG​(xi​)∣∣G∣​,
(20)
where Z(G) is the center of a group and CG​(xi​) is the centralizer of xi​. Each central element contributes its own one-element conjugacy class. Every remaining conjugacy class contributes its size, given by the orbit-stabilizer theorem. The sum counts each element exactly once. See McKernan, Group actions and automorphisms, lemma 23.6.
For conjugacy classes of the symmetric group on three letters, take x1​=(12) and x2​=(123). Their centralizers have sizes two and three, and the center of a group has size one, giving
6=1+26​+36​=1+3+2.
(21)
For an abelian group, every centralizer is the whole group, every conjugacy class has size one, and the sum over noncentral representatives is empty.
The power of this counting identity is that the sizes of conjugacy classes constrain group structure. For a nontrivial finite p-group with group order pn, every noncentral conjugacy class has size a positive power of p, by Lagrange's theorem. The class equation therefore gives ∣Z(G)∣≡0(modp). Since the identity element lies in the center of a group, the center of a group must have at least p elements. This obtains an element commuting with the entire group without constructing one. See McKernan, lemma 23.7.
Historically, these ideas belong to the nineteenth-century development of permutation groups and normal subgroups. Milne's historical opening records Galois's introduction of normal subgroups in 1832 and Jordan's systematic treatment of permutation groups in 1870. This is context for the conjugation action and the class equation, rather than a claim that either author first stated the modern formula.[ref]

Centralizer and normalizer

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Conjugation action OurBigBook.com
Both constructions are stabilizer subgroups for the conjugation action. The centralizer CG​(x) fixes an individual element x; the normalizer NG​(H) preserves a subgroup H as a whole, while possibly moving its elements. The centralizer of a subset CG​(H) fixes every member of H individually, so
CG​(H)⊆NG​(H).
(22)
For a cyclic subgroup H=⟨r⟩, commuting with the group generator r is equivalent to commuting with all its powers, giving CG​(H)=CG​(r).
In the symmetric group S3​, let r=(123) and H=⟨r⟩={e,(123),(132)}. Then
CS3​​(r)=CS3​​(H)=H,NS3​​(H)=S3​.
(23)
Every transposition sends r to r−1 under conjugation. In particular, for t=(12),
trt−1=r−1=r,tHt−1={e,r−1,r}=H.
(24)
Thus t belongs to the normalizer of H but not to the centralizer of r. Preserving the collection of powers allows the two possible directions of its group generator to be exchanged.
This distinction lets one ask separately which operations leave a chosen operation unchanged and which operations preserve the subgroup it generates. The normalizer also supplies a group homomorphism to the automorphism group of H, by g↦(h↦ghg−1); its group kernel is CG​(H). In this example the group homomorphism has two possible outputs, fixing r or replacing it by r−1. The quotient group NS3​​(H)/CS3​​(H) is therefore a cyclic group of group order two. Milne develops the normalizer as a stabilizer subgroup in Group Theory (v4.01) by James S. Milne.

Centralizer (CG​(x))

Words: 662 Articles: 4
Centralizer and normalizer OurBigBook.com
The centralizer of an element x of a group G consists of all elements that commute with x:
CG​(x)={g∈G:gx=xg}={g∈G:gxg−1=x}.
(25)
It is the stabilizer subgroup of x under the conjugation action, hence a subgroup of G. In conjugacy classes of the symmetric group on three letters, the three representative computations are
CS3​​(e)=S3​,CS3​​((12))={e,(12)},CS3​​((123))={e,(123),(132)}.
(26)
For the transposition (12), a commuting permutation must preserve the exchanged pair {1,2} and fix 3; only e and (12) do so. For r=(123), a commuting permutation is determined by where it sends 1: the equation g(r(i))=r(g(i)) forces the images of 2 and 3, leaving exactly e,r,r2. For e, every permutation commutes. These centralizer sizes 6,2,3 give conjugacy class sizes 1,3,2.
The centralizer is useful because it measures how much freedom remains after fixing one operation. Its index of a subgroup counts the distinct results of conjugation, and the intersection of all element centralizers is the center of a group. A centralizer need not be an abelian group: CG​(e)=G even when G is a nonabelian group. In an abelian group, all element centralizers equal G. These observations also explain why the surrounding group matters: the centralizer of (123) inside the alternating group A3​ is the whole A3​, whereas its centralizer inside S3​ is a proper subgroup. See McKernan, the centralizer definition preceding lemma 23.6.
For an arbitrary subset A⊆G, the centralizer of a subset fixes every element of A individually under the conjugation action:
CG​(A)={g∈G:ga=ag for all a∈A}=⋂a∈A​CG​(a).
(27)
This is a pointwise stabilizer of the elements of A, not of the vertices of a polygon in a geometric realization. In particular, r=(123) belongs to CS3​​(r) although its rotation moves every vertex of a polygon of the equilateral triangle. If A generates a subgroup H, commuting with every element of A implies commuting with every product of those elements and their inverse elements; hence CG​(A)=CG​(H). For the triangle rotation subgroup H=⟨r⟩, this gives CS3​​(H)=CS3​​(r)=H.
To see the commutation test directly on the equilateral triangle, compare a rotation r with the reflection s=(12). Their permutations satisfy
rs=(13),sr=(23),srs−1=r−1.

A group action is faithful when only the identity acts as the identity on every point.
For a group action of G on a set X, form the group homomorphism

(41)
A faithful group action means that ρ is injective: different group elements induce different permutations of X. Equivalently, its group kernel is trivial:

Here Gx​ is the stabilizer subgroup of x, and e is the identity element.[ref]
The test is global. A faithful group action requires each nonidentity group element to move at least one point; a free group action requires it to move every point. In the faithful coset action of the symmetric group on three letters, (12) fixes one coset and exchanges the other two. Thus a nontrivial stabilizer subgroup does not rule out faithfulness. The distinction follows directly from the order of the quantifiers:
faithful: ∀g=e ∃x: g⋅x=x,free: ∀g=e ∀x: g⋅x=x.
(43)
On a nonempty set, a free group action is therefore a faithful group action. A transitive group action instead asks whether every point can reach every other; it allows several group elements to perform exactly the same rearrangement. The nonfaithful coset action of the symmetric group on three letters is a counterexample to the claim that every transitive group action is a faithful group action.

If K={e}, this forces g=h; if K contains a nonidentity element, that element and e act identically. Thus a faithful group action turns G into an actual subgroup of a symmetric group, retaining its group operation as function composition. Choosing a suitable coset action can give a much smaller set of labels than the regular group action used in Cayley's theorem.

Between these extremes, a nontrivial subgroup with trivial subgroup core can give a faithful group action on fewer labels. If the index of a subgroup is finite, [G:H]=n, the first isomorphism theorem gives
G/CoreG​(H)≅imρH​≤Sn​.
(52)
Thus a subgroup of small index of a subgroup exposes a small permutation group associated with G. The two examples below and in nonfaithful coset action of the symmetric group on three letters show exactly which information can survive.

Faithful coset action of the symmetric group on three letters (CoreS3​​(⟨(12)⟩)={e})

Words: 222
Coset action OurBigBook.com
Take the symmetric group G=S3​ and the subgroup H=⟨(12)⟩={e,(12)} of group order two. With the rightmost permutation applied first, its three left cosets are
C3​=H={e,(12)},C2​=(23)H={(23),(132)},C1​=(13)H={(13),(123)}.
(53)
The subscripts record the image of 3: every member of Ci​ sends 3 to i. Because H is the stabilizer subgroup of 3 in the usual group action, aH↦a(3) is a bijection onto {1,2,3}. It is an equivariant map, since (ga)(3)=g(a(3)). The coset action therefore becomes the familiar group action on three letters. In particular,
(12):C1​↔C2​, C3​↦C3​,(123):C1​↦C2​↦C3​↦C1​.
(54)
The three stabilizer subgroups are
GC1​​={e,(23)},GC2​​={e,(13)},GC3​​={e,(12)}.
(55)
Their intersection is {e}, so the subgroup core and the group kernel are trivial. This proves that the coset action is a faithful group action even though every point has a nontrivial stabilizer subgroup. The orbit-stabilizer theorem reads 6=3⋅2, while the induced group homomorphism gives six distinct permutations of the three cosets. For example, (12) and e agree at C3​, but disagree at C1​; inspecting one label would miss their difference.
The subgroup need not be a normal subgroup for the coset action to exist: (123)H(123)−1={e,(23)}=H. Here the group action is informative because the three conjugate stabilizer subgroups have no common nonidentity element. For the normal subgroup A3​ instead, nonfaithful coset action of the symmetric group on three letters shows that only the sign of a permutation survives.
